questions.question: Explain, step by step, how orographic rain and a rain shadow form, using a South African example.
questions.expected_answer: Moist air from the sea blows towards a mountain range and is forced to rise up the windward side. As it rises, pressure falls, it expands and cools. When it reaches its dew point, water vapour condenses into cloud, and further rising produces rain or snow on the windward side. The air crosses the summit having lost much moisture; descending the leeward side, it is compressed and warms, at about 10 °C per 1 000 m when dry, so it can hold more moisture and clouds evaporate; the leeward side is dry, a rain shadow. Example: in winter, north-westerly winds with cold fronts give Newlands on the windward Cape Fold Mountains about 1 500 mm, while Worcester in the Breede valley gets about 250 mm, about six times less.

questions.question: Compare the climates of Mthatha and Durban and explain the differences, separating the effect of relief from other factors.
questions.expected_answer: Durban, at sea level on the coast at about 30 degrees south, gets about 1 000 mm of rain, with a January mean of about 24.5 °C, July about 17 °C and a range of about 7.5 °C. Mthatha, about 75 km inland at about 700 m and 31.5 degrees south, gets about 650 mm, with January about 21 °C, July about 12 °C and a range of 9 °C. Relief: moist Indian Ocean air from the east and south-east rises over the coastal hills and higher ground, dropping much of its rain nearer the coast, so less reaches Mthatha, which relies more on summer thunderstorms. Temperature: Mthatha's altitude makes it about 4.5 °C cooler; its inland position gives a larger range and colder nights; Durban has the warm Agulhas Current.

questions.question: Explain how slope aspect and mountain barriers affect climate.
questions.expected_answer: Aspect: in the southern hemisphere the midday sun is in the northern sky, especially in winter, so north-facing slopes receive more direct sunlight and are warmer and drier, while south-facing slopes are cooler, shadier and damper, often with thicker vegetation and longer-lasting snow; people place vineyards and orchards according to aspect, and highveld houses face north to catch winter sun. In the northern hemisphere south-facing slopes are sunnier. Barriers: mountains block or redirect air masses; the Great Escarpment limits moist east-coast air reaching the interior; the Himalayas block cold central Asian air and force monsoon winds to rise, giving heavy rain. Mountains also create valley breezes by day and mountain breezes by night, with cold air collecting in valleys and causing frost and inversions.
